pages.x: After the war Germany and its capital were split between the Allies. In 1948 Stalin closed the roads into West Berlin to starve it into his hands, and for almost a year American and British planes flew in food and coal, landing every few minutes. In 1949 Germany split into two states, the democratic West and the communist East.

By 1961 some two and a half million East Germans had fled west, many of them through Berlin. On the night of 13 August 1961 East German soldiers and workers strung barbed wire across the city, and soon a concrete wall went up. Families were cut off from each other overnight.

The wall grew into two walls, with sand, watchtowers, dogs and searchlights between them. At least 140 people were killed trying to cross. Others escaped through tunnels, in secret car compartments, by hot-air balloon and over the rooftops. In 1962 Peter Fechter, 18, was shot and left to bleed to death in sight of the West.

In June 1963 President Kennedy came to West Berlin and told a crowd of hundreds of thousands that every free person was a citizen of Berlin, and that he was proud to say, in German, I am a Berliner. In 1987 President Ronald Reagan stood at the wall and told the Soviet leader to tear it down.

In the 1980s the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev began reforms and made it clear he would not send tanks to keep Eastern Europe communist. In 1989 Poland held free elections, Hungary opened its border with Austria, and East Germans poured west through it. In Leipzig crowds marched every Monday, chanting we are the people.

On the evening of 9 November an East German spokesman, muddling a new rule, told reporters that people could cross the border at once. Thousands rushed to the checkpoints, and the overwhelmed guards opened the gates. Berliners danced on the wall and chipped pieces off it with hammers.
Less than a year later, on 3 October 1990, the two Germanys were united again. Within two years communist rule had ended across Eastern Europe, and the Soviet Union itself was gone.

The Berlin Wall was the symbol of the Cold War, the split between the communist East and the democratic West, and its fall was the moment that split ended. A few stretches still stand as memorials, and pieces of it are kept in museums around the world.
